body: I'd like to make sure we get to https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12304 this time.
I would like to discuss the proposed fetch behavior of https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11687

-   **Administrative Announcements**: Chris Wilson announced they will be leaving Google as of April 19.
- **Popover Hint Inconsistent Behavior (Issue 12304):** Jake Archibald introduced a carryover issue regarding inconsistent behavior in nested versus unnested popover hints. They and Mason Freed have tentatively agreed on a path forward regarding the behaviors and inconsistencies they discovered while trying to explain the difference between `popover=hint` and `popover=auto`. A key inconsistency is that at the top level, hints and autos can show simultaneously, but in a nested situation, showing a hint hides the other auto. Jake Archibald presented several desired changes to popover hint behavior, including allowing a hint and an auto popover to show at the same time in nested situations, resolving exclusivity. Another change proposed is that showing a hint should close other unrelated hints unless they are parents. The presenters also sought to change the behavior where hiding an auto popover currently closes all hint popovers, suggesting it should only close children popovers and nothing else. The current behavior is that clicking outside a popover will close it, which applies to both auto and hint types. A discovered inconsistency is that clicking inside a hint does not close an auto popover nested within the hint, and the proposal is to change this behavior so that the generic rule (clicking outside hides the popover) is consistently applied. A weird behavior was identified where attempting to show an auto popover inside a hint popover makes the hint disappear, and anchor positioning fails because of incorrect rendering order. The proposed fix is to prevent this action, so that calling `showPopover` in this case should throw an exception, and doing it via a declarative button or select element should no-op and log to the console. Keith Cirkel expressed slight reservation about the throwing mechanism for declarative cases, suggesting it might be difficult for developers to debug. Mason Freed agreed with the solution to either throw an error or use a console log instead of using "magical promotion" of popover types, reasoning that developers will open dev tools and see the console warning. The discussion noted that the declarative case currently lacks JavaScript to throw into, but it might be possible to report an error to the console and fire an `onerror` event listener, which would make the error visible in production tools. Simon Pieters raised a concern about select elements within hints, as this could be broken if the exception route is taken, because the base select element acts like a `popover=auto`. The issue of how select elements behave within a hint popover was raised, noting that the base select element functions as a `popover=auto`. It was acknowledged that if they commit to the rule that hints cannot have subordinate autos, then hints could not contain select elements, which might be a reason to reconsider the exception route. The group agreed to separate the discussion about the nested auto/hint conflict resolution (Option 5) into a separate issue, while moving forward with the rest of the agreed-upon changes.
- **HTML in Canvas: High Contrast Mode and Password Behavior**: pdr@  provided updates on the HTML and canvas proposal, addressing feedback from the last meeting. It was determined that high contrast mode will be exposed in HTML and canvas due to the high user benefit. Regarding passwords, no new information would be exposed; if JavaScript can read the password, HTML and canvas can read it, but if JavaScript cannot see password information (including manager options), HTML and canvas also cannot. PDR@ reported positive validations from Microsoft, Igalia, and Google accessibility experts regarding the API, and they plan to engage the ARIA working group. Addressing Simon Frasier's feedback from Apple, it was confirmed that snapshotting elements (needed for painting) has a cost, but this cost is already paid by the browser for visible elements. It was clarified that elements not intended for painting should be removed from the DOM or set to `display: none` to ensure accessibility and avoid unnecessary snapshotting costs. Drawing elements should ideally occur in the paint event to keep the frame in sync with surrounding DOM content, though the API can be called at any time (potentially getting the previous frame's rendering). The quality of implementation for scaling (pixelation vs. vector-based rendering) is not firmly specified, but the current implementation uses vectors, which someone in Design On A Dime (us-sfo-fre215) agreed should be the standard to avoid interop issues. Styling works the same inside the canvas as it does outside, ensuring accessibility and hit testing are consistent. Clipping is set to the border box by default, but an API option (called the source rect) is available to expand the clipping area to include ink overflow, which is useful for elements like focus rings. All elements are exposed to hit testing and accessibility, meaning content not being shown to the user should be removed from the DOM. PDR@ confirmed that security concerns related to extensions like OnePassword and LastPass have been checked, and the API exposes no new information that is not already available to JavaScript. These extensions use cross-origin iframes, preventing the page's JavaScript from accessing content, and HTML in canvas also cannot access this content. Furthermore, cross-origin content does not paint in HTML canvas, which is critical for the API's security.
- **HTML in Canvas: Complex Hit Testing Demo and API Consideration:** Jake Archibald demonstrated a technique for complex hit testing (like curved elements) by moving the underlying element on pointer move, which allows for text selection, link opening, and form fields to work. PDR@ asked if a more explicit API should be added, noting that existing issues like anchor positioning and focus states might be solvable with a new API. A concern raised by others was the potential for running JavaScript in the middle of a hit test, which could create issues by modifying the DOM. Kurt Catti-Schmidt verified that the HTML and canvas proposal will not expose more information about file input paths than is already available via JavaScript. Modern file inputs only show the last file name in the UI, which is difficult to scrape via OCR. Kurt Catti-Schmidt also confirmed that basic input and Windows screen reader functionality (e.g., move by word/character) worked in a demo of the API. Smaug raised concerns about the latency between the main thread and the worker when using offscreen canvas with this API. The current approach uses the lowest-level primitive, allowing developers to post message the snapshotted elements to an offscreen canvas worker thread from the `onpaint` event. Someone in Design On A Dime (us-sfo-fre215) acknowledged that latency is inherent to using threads and post messages, allowing developers to prioritize input latency or smoothness. Smaug worried that the current API might not work well in workers due to post message latency and suggested exploring a scheduling API or a bypass mechanism to prioritize synchronization. Someone in Design On A Dime (us-sfo-fre215) agreed that solving post message latency for events is important but questioned if the solution should be specific to this API or a lower-level primitive. The core concern is that DOM updates and visual representation may not be synced, which affects hit testing. Keith Cirkel expressed that Mozilla needs more time for an internal, formal discussion before moving the API to Stage 2, citing concerns about web compatibility and potential new fingerprinting vectors due to trivial readback. Chris Wilson clarified that Stage 2 means committing to solving the problem with a rough design, expecting refinements, and is not the point of implementation/shipping (Stage 3). Keith Cirkel further explained that committing to the API shape without readback might undermine the feature's core use cases, creating developer pressure, and therefore they need to ensure the API is in the right shape. PDR@ noted that drawing gradients and text into canvas via the widely-used foreign object approach already presents similar fingerprinting risks, and mitigations developed for that can apply to this new, more ergonomic API. The group agreed to hold the HTML and canvas discussion over until the next meeting, allowing time for Mozilla to conduct their internal formal discussion and potentially resolve the large-scale question of readback.
- **Selected Content Removal Steps (Issue 12906)**: Joey Arhar provided an update on an issue regarding modifying the DOM during the selected content element's insertion or removal steps. The problem arises with option elements because their insertion/removal can trigger a change in selection, which then updates the selected content element during the option element's steps. Possible solutions include updating the selected content element in the option element's post-insertion steps or posting a task for later update, but the discussion was held over pending feedback from Anna.
- **Focus Group Declarative Keyboard Focus Navigation (Issue 11641):** Jacques Newman provided a brief update, calling for review of the specification and updated standards positions from WebKit and Mozilla. The spec has been updated to align with the latest Open UI explainer.
- **Platform Provided Behaviors for Custom Elements (Issue 12150):** Ana Sollano Kim presented a proposal for allowing custom elements to adopt native behaviors using `attachInternals` to accept a list of behaviors, starting with `submit`. The discussion centered on two proposed API shapes for defining the behaviors. Keith Cirkel and Ana Sollano Kim agreed that the current proposed option, which allows the author to hold direct references to behaviors, is preferable to an alternative that requires an additional behaviors interface.  Ana Sollano Kim plans to close out remaining open questions, including renaming "behaviors" and, more importantly, resolving conflict resolutions for multiple behaviors. They intend to file a TAG review soon and have already filed browser signals.
- **Declarative CSS Modules (Incomplete Discussion):** Kurt Catti-Schmidt quickly introduced an update to the proposal for the `shadowRoot adoptedStyleSheets` attribute. The explainer has been updated to include fetch behavior, with a plan to use placeholder empty stylesheets for each fetch to manage out-of-order fetching, which are then replaced once the fetch completes. Kurt Catti-Schmidt proposed two approaches for handling CSS module scripts, both aimed at managing stylesheet order during asynchronous fetching and mutation. The first proposal involved maintaining the original specified order while allowing adopted stylesheets to mutate, which would permit inserting a stylesheet (B) while others (A and C) are being fetched, keeping them all in the correct relative order. The second option involved creating a final placeholder before the initial fetch and having the module map update using a `replace sync` on the style, which alters module fetching specifically for CSS module scripts and avoids the placeholder issue while preserving desired behaviors. Keith Cirkel expressed concerns about the first approach, suggesting it sounded strange and might create garbage collection pressure from creating and discarding objects. They found the second option, where the stylesheet is created by the system and uses `replace sync`, to be more intuitive, noting that developers could polyfill this behavior today. Kurt Catti-Schmidt agreed with the preference for the second approach, confirming they would proceed with it and update the explainer and specification documents. Kurt Catti-Schmidt mentioned the current explainer describes the placeholder behavior, which they checked into Chromium last week, but noted that this initial implementation has an issue where retrieving a reference before completion results in a non-equivalent stylesheet object after completion. They confirmed they have a prototype for the second, preferred approach and will work on checking it in and updating the explainer and specification.
- **Meeting Conclusion and Next Steps:** Chris Wilson concluded the meeting due to time constraints. The last two agenda items were postponed and moved to the next meeting.
